paragraphs: Betzat nebela shennitnabbela bishchita, "g demutteret min hattora - asaruha chaza"l kemo hannebela atzmah, kevan shebbaa min hannebela shehi asura min hattora. vaapillu nigmera legamre dikyotze bah nimkeret bashshuq, asura; vaapillu nitareba beelep, kullam asurot; abal betzat terepa asura min hattora, mippene shennigmera beissur, deshemma beshaa shennitrepa hattarnegolet hayeta habbetza raq basar, velo nigmera baet hahi ella aach"k, venimtza shennigmera beissur. vaapillu yadeinan shello nitrepa hattarnegolet ella rega echad qodem shennishchata, apillu hake asura min hattora, shello natenu chakamim dibrehem lisorim. umeachar debazzeman hazzeh darkam limkor habbetzim beminyan tamid, laken apillu nitareba beelep enah betela.

clarification.explanation: An egg laid by a nevelah chicken (slaughtered improperly and thereby forbidden) — although by strict Torah law the egg itself would be permitted (since the egg is separate from the mother's body), the Sages forbade it by decree, like the nevelah itself, since it comes from a Torah-forbidden source. This holds true even if the egg has already fully formed (to the point of being sold in the market normally), and even if it became mixed with a thousand other eggs — all become forbidden (it is not nullified in the majority). By contrast, the egg of a treifah fowl is forbidden by actual Torah law, since there is concern that at the time the fowl became treifah, the egg was not yet complete (it was still merely "flesh"), and only completed afterward, while the chicken was already treifah — so the egg "was completed in a state of prohibition." And even if it is known the fowl became treifah one moment before slaughter, the egg is still Torah-forbidden, since the Sages did not establish precise time measures in this matter. Since nowadays it is customary to sell eggs by count (not by weight), a forbidden egg mixed even with a thousand others is not nullified at all.
takeaways: A nevelah's egg is only rabbinically forbidden, yet is not nullified even among a thousand — since it is considered a "whole item" sold by count.
A treifah's egg is actually Torah-forbidden, out of concern it completed forming while the fowl was already treifah.
Even a one-moment gap between the treifah condition and slaughter does not suffice to permit it.

paragraphs: Tarnegolet shennishchata venimtzea terepa, veyesh betzim shennoledu mimmenna qodem shennishchata: im hi terepa sheepshar shello era lah ella atta, kegon shenniqqab qerum shel mocha vekayyotze - habbetzim muttarim, deamerinan hashta hu denitrepa; abal im yadua denitrepa qodem sheyyaleda habbetzim, kegon yeteret ebar shennitrepa bo, o shehuglad pi hammakka shebbeyadua sheshshelosha yamim qodem shechita haya bazeh zeh hatterepot, mippene shei epshar lehaggeled pachot mishshelosha yamim, az kol habbetzim shennoledu mimmenna asurot, vaapillu otam shennoledu qodem shelosha yamim, name asurot; dekol mah shennolad mimmenna betok y"b chodesh qodem shennishchata, asurim; abal mah shennolad qodem y"b chodesh, muttar veen bo sapeq kelal, mippene sheyyadua dehatterepa enah chayya y"b chodesh, vekannizkar kol zeh besiman p", bedin haggebina. v"g dehatam rama" za"l behaggahat hashshulchan hittir behuglad pi hammakka mah shennaasa mimmenna qodem shelosha yamim, velo asar ella behannolad tok shelosha yamim - hinneh mera"n za"l dato leesor ap shennolad venaasa qodem shelosha yamim, vekannizkar bashsha"k uperi chadash uperi toar ushear acharonim sham besiman p". velaken ledidan deqibbalnu horaat maran za"l, tzarik leesor kemo shekkatabnu leel; mihu, katabti bsh"q "mqbtzl": behuglad pi hammakka, veenah nitrepet terepot vadday meotah makka, ella hu sepeq terepot, az kol habbetzim shennoledu qodem shelosha yamim muttarim mikkoach sepeq sepeqa, vehu: sapeq noleda qodem, sapeq noleda aach"k; veim timtze lomar aach"k, shemma en kan terepot; usepeq sapeqa zeh hu mithappek; veod asiti sepeq sepeqa beopen acher.

clarification.explanation: A chicken slaughtered and found treifah, having eggs laid before slaughter: if the treifah condition is of a type that could have occurred one moment before slaughter (for example, a perforation of the brain membrane) — all the eggs laid beforehand are permitted, since one assumes the treifah condition occurred only now. But if it is known the chicken was already treifah before laying the eggs (for example, a wound that had begun to scab, which takes at least three days) — then all eggs laid from the moment the treifah condition arose until slaughter are forbidden, including those laid even before those three days. The rule: any egg laid within the twelve months before slaughter is forbidden, out of concern the chicken was already treifah then; but an egg laid more than twelve months before slaughter is permitted without any doubt, since it is known a treifah animal cannot live twelve months. The Ben Ish Chai notes a dispute between the Rema and Maran (the Shulchan Aruch) regarding the scabbing: the Rema permits what was laid before the three days, while Maran (whose view is accepted by us) forbids those too. But if there is only doubt about the treifah condition (not certainty), the Ben Ish Chai notes he wrote elsewhere that one may be lenient regarding eggs laid before the three days, by force of a "double doubt."
takeaways: If the treifah condition could be new (a moment before slaughter) — the earlier eggs are permitted.
If the treifah condition is known to be old (such as a scabbed wound, taking 3 days) — all eggs from the 12 months before slaughter are forbidden.
An egg laid more than twelve months before slaughter is permitted without doubt, since a treifah animal cannot live that long.

paragraphs: Betza shehi sapeq im hi betzat terepa o im hi betzat keshera, hare zo asura, mishshum dehave sepeqa deorayeta ulechumera; abal sapeq im hi betzat nebela o betzat keshera, mutteret, dispeqa derabbanan lequlla. veken hu haddin betarnegolet sheyyesh sapeq im hi nebela o shechuta kegon sapeq bashshechita, habbetza shellah mutteret, mishshum dehave sapeqa derabbanan. veayyen bashsha"k, seip-qatan y", uperi chadash v"peri-toar" vesipte daat vechakemat adam ushear acharonim.

clarification.explanation: If there is doubt regarding a particular egg — whether it is a treifah's egg or a kosher egg — the egg is forbidden, since this is a doubt in Torah law (the treifah prohibition being Torah-level), and a Torah-level doubt is resolved stringently. But if the doubt is whether it is a nevelah's egg or a kosher egg — the egg is permitted, since the prohibition of a nevelah's egg is only rabbinic, and a rabbinic doubt is resolved leniently. Likewise, if there is doubt about the chicken itself — whether it is a nevelah or properly slaughtered (for example, doubt about the validity of the slaughter) — its egg is permitted, since this too is considered a rabbinic doubt.
takeaways: Doubt whether an egg is a treifah's egg — forbidden (a Torah-level doubt, resolved stringently).
Doubt whether an egg is a nevelah's egg — permitted (a rabbinic doubt, resolved leniently).
Doubt about the validity of the slaughter itself — the chicken's egg is permitted, since this too is a rabbinic doubt.

paragraphs: "g debetzat nebela asura midderabbanan - apillu im nitareba beelep, kullam asurot mishshum kevan dehi betzat nebela, bevadday ittachzaq issura velo batel, ukemo shekkatebu bashsha"k uperi chadash vesipte daat ushear acharonim za"l.

clarification.explanation: Even though the prohibition of a nevelah's egg is only rabbinic (not Torah-level), if it becomes mixed even with a thousand other eggs — all become forbidden, and it is not nullified in the majority. The reason: since it is certainly a nevelah's egg whose prohibition is fixed ("the prohibition is established"), and eggs are considered "a counted item" — that is, sold and counted in units, not by weight — and the halachic rule is that a counted item is not nullified in a mixture even among a thousand (as explained above in halacha 1).
takeaways: A mixed-in nevelah's egg is not nullified even among a thousand, since it is considered "a counted item" (eggs sold and counted by unit, not weight).

paragraphs: Ha deamerinan: betza shennoleda mittarnegolet shehi sepeq nebela deara lah sapeq bashshechita demutteret habbetza mishshum dehave sapeq derabbanan - haynu davqa im hassapeq hu sapeq shaha o sapeq daras, o sheshshachat besakkin peguma - bazeh amerinan mutteret habbetza; abal im hassapeq hu mishshum dela badaq hassimanim im shachat harob o lav, hare zo chashiba vadday nebela vehabbetza shellah asura, ukemo shekkatab sipte daat, siman p"v, seip qatan y".

clarification.explanation: The rule stated earlier — that an egg from a chicken with doubtful nevelah status (doubt about the validity of the slaughter) is permitted since this is a rabbinic doubt — is true only when the doubt is of the ordinary kind: doubt whether the slaughterer "paused" too long during slaughter, or "pressed" with the knife, or the knife was flawed. But if the doubt is because the signs of slaughter were not examined at all (and it is not known whether most of the trachea and esophagus were cut) — in such a case the chicken is considered certainly nevelah (since no examination was performed at all), and its egg is likewise forbidden.
takeaways: Doubt about the validity of the slaughter (pausing, pressing, a flawed knife) — the egg is permitted, a rabbinic doubt.
A complete lack of examination of the signs (not checked whether properly slaughtered) — the chicken is considered certainly nevelah, and the egg is forbidden.

paragraphs: En mokerin betzat nebela uterepa legoy, shemma yimkerenna leyisrael. ketzad yaaseh? yitrepenna biqara veyimkerenna. v"g dekatab mvr"m za"l: en mokerin betza terupa legoy shemma yearebenna bepat - hinneh poh irenu bagdad y" nahagu kisbarat mera"n za"l limkor betzim terupot legoy. v"g depat bebetzim la shekicha beirenu, im kol zeh shekicha latet betzim bemine metiqa; ki kaasher mesannenin hassoker laasot mimmennu mine metiqa, mannichin bo chelbon betzim; veken od bimtiqa sheqqorin "min el samma" (min hashshamayim - mematteq millachluchit ale etzim) mannichin gam ken loben-betza, veim kol zeh nahagu limkor betza terupa legoy, "p sheqqonim mine metiqa hannizkarim min haggoyim. veha deqonin mine metiqa min haggoyim veen chosheshin shemma yesh bahem betzat nebela, haynu mishshum deazelinan batar rubba.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to sell a nevelah's or treifah's egg to a gentile, out of concern the gentile might resell it to a Jew by mistake (without knowing it is forbidden). What is done? The egg is beaten (mixed) in a bowl so it is recognizably no longer whole, and then sold to the gentile — since now there is no concern it will be resold to a Jew as an ordinary egg. The Rema wrote that even a beaten egg should not be sold to a gentile, out of concern he might mix it into bread later sold to a Jew. But in Baghdad the custom followed Maran's (the Shulchan Aruch's) lenient view, selling beaten eggs to a gentile, since there is no local custom of mixing eggs into bread. Nevertheless, there is a common custom of putting egg white into certain sweets (such as when refining sugar, or in the sweet "man al-sama"), and yet the custom is to sell a beaten egg to a gentile, and even to buy these sweets from gentiles without concern, since one follows the majority (most eggs used for sweetening are kosher eggs).
takeaways: It is forbidden to sell a whole nevelah's/treifah's egg to a gentile, out of concern it will be resold to a Jew; this is resolved by beating the egg in a bowl.
The Baghdad custom is lenient, selling a beaten egg to a gentile (unlike the Rema's stricter view).
Sweets containing egg white may be bought from gentiles, since one follows the majority.

paragraphs: En liqnot betza terupa min haggoy, deshemma yisrael makar lo betzat nebela uterepa uterapan. v"g dehaacharonim za"l katebu deen issur liqnot betzim terupot miggoy ella-im-ken terupot legamre, shemmeorabim hachelbonim vehachelmonim yachad, abal im hi raq shebura vehachelbon vehachelmon shelemim, muttar liqnot; im kol zeh poh irenu bagdad y" nahagu shello liqnot apillu bikhe gavna dechelbon vechelmon shelemim.

clarification.explanation: One should not buy a beaten egg from a gentile, out of concern that a Jew sold him a nevelah's or treifah's egg, and the gentile beat it (in order to resell it). The later authorities wrote that the prohibition applies specifically to a fully beaten egg, that is, when the white and yolk are mixed together; but an egg only cracked on the outside (the shell split) while the white and yolk remain whole and separate inside — is permitted to buy. Nevertheless, in Baghdad the custom was to be stringent and not buy even such an egg (with whole white and yolk), but only eggs entirely whole in their shell.
takeaways: One should not buy a beaten egg (white and yolk mixed) from a gentile, out of concern it is a nevelah's/treifah's egg beaten to conceal this.
An egg cracked on the outside but whole inside is by strict law permitted to buy, but the Baghdad custom was to be stringent about this too.

paragraphs: Betza sheyyesh lah shene chelmonim mutteret, ukemo shekkatab bemachaziq beraka, ot b', ushear acharonim. ubetza sheen bah ella chelbon bilbad: im hi qetanna beyoter, nimtzet balul hattarnegolim bebet yisrael, mutteret; abal im enah qetanna meod, ella raq qetanna meat mechabroteha, en lehattir. veim hebiah goy, apillu qetanna meod en lehattir; veayyen machaziq beraka za"l.

clarification.explanation: An egg with two yolks is entirely permitted with no concern. An egg containing only white with no yolk at all — if it is very small and found in a Jew's home chicken coop, it is permitted (since it is recognizably a normal, simple product of the coop); but if the egg is not very small, only slightly smaller than the other eggs, it should not be permitted. And if such an egg was brought by a gentile — even if very small, it should not be permitted at all (since there is no assurance it is from a known Jewish coop).
takeaways: An egg with two yolks is permitted without concern.
An egg with white only and no yolk is permitted only if very small and from a Jewish home coop; from a gentile it is forbidden even if very small.

paragraphs: Betzat op tame, veken betzat terepa o nebela shennitbashshela im betzim kesherot: im hi biqlippatah, enah oseret, sheen koach bebishshul lehotzi gup haasur derek haqqelippa; umah sheyyotze derek haqqelippa en bo mammash, raq mayya debee bealema ihu; abal im betzat haissur qelupa o nequba - apillu im betzim hakkesherot odan biqlippatan, hare zo oseret, vetzarik s" (shishshim veechad) betzim shel hetter kenegdah lebattelah - ben shehi shelema umakkirah ben shehi terupa. v"g dekol haissurin shiuran beshishshim - hechmiru chaza"l bebetzim, mishshum sheyyesh bahem gedolim uqetannim, lekak hosipu achat. veim nitbashshela betza zo haasura shehi qelupa o nequba betok hattabshil, en tzarik ella shishshim battabshil lebattala. vekol zeh hu lebattel pelitatah, abal hi atzmah enah betela vaasura. veen meshaarin betza haasura ella keneged mah sheyyesh betokah, abal keneged haqqelippa shellah en tzarik, veadderabba, qelippatah mitztarepet im hahetter lebattel haissur, shehare kullam boleim hattaam beshaveh.

clarification.explanation: A forbidden fowl's egg, or a treifah's or nevelah's egg, cooked together with kosher eggs: if the forbidden egg is still whole in its shell (fully closed), it does not forbid the other eggs — since cooking is not powerful enough to draw the forbidden substance out through the intact shell; whatever does emerge through it is considered "mere water" with no significance. But if the forbidden egg is peeled, opened, or perforated — it does forbid, even if the kosher eggs are still in their shells, and sixty-one (61) kosher eggs are needed against the forbidden egg to nullify it (whether it is whole or beaten). The reason one extra unit is added to the ordinary measure of sixty: since eggs vary in size (large and small), the Sages were stringent and added one more unit. If the forbidden egg was cooked within a dish (not merely with other eggs), sixty within the dish suffices to nullify it. All this concerns nullifying the taste that emerged from it, but the egg itself, even after nullification, remains forbidden. The measure for nullification is calculated only against what is inside the egg, not against its shell — and in practice the shell itself counts toward the permitted side (since all absorb the taste equally).
takeaways: A forbidden egg remaining whole and closed in its shell during cooking forbids nothing.
A peeled or perforated forbidden egg forbids, requiring 61 kosher eggs to nullify it (not 60, due to size variation).
Even after nullification, the forbidden egg itself remains forbidden — only the taste that emerged from it is nullified.

paragraphs: Ha deamerinan: im betzat haissur odenna shelema biqlippatah sheenah nequba, deenah oseret, haynu davqa bebetzat op tame o betzat terepa o nebela; abal betza sheyyesh bah eprocha, oseret "p sheenah qelupa kelal, mippene shehaeprocha hu nebela. veken hu haddin im hi betza shennimtza bah dam al hachelmon, gam-ken oseret apillu enah qelupa, detippat haddam hu hatchalat riqqum haeprocha, ushede tikla bekol habbetza; hilkak hattaam sheyyotze mimmenna hu taam basar nebela mammash, veoseret apillu enah qelupa. mihu leinyan shiur habbittul im nitbashshela battabshil: im hi betza sheyyesh bah dam, saggi lah beshishshim kenegdah lebattelah; veim hi betza sheyyesh bah eprocha shennitbashshela battabshil - yesh omerim shetztzarik echad veshishshim kenegdah, mishshum dehave keen birya, umechamat chashibutah hosipu lah cheleq echad yoter; veyesh omerim, gam betza shennimtza bah eprocha shennitbashshela betabshil shel hetter, saggi lah beshishshim; ubehepsed merubbeh o sheat haddechaq, yesh lehaqel kedibrehem. veayyen mishbetzot zahab, sop seip qatan y"g, v"erek-hashshulchan", sop ot d', ushear acharonim. ukebar katabnu leel: ben nishleqa im habbetzim, ben nitbashshela betabshil shel hetter - mitztarepim haqqelippot lebattel haissur; vehu haddin haka bebetzat eprocha o betzat dam bachelmon, demitztarepin qelippa shellahem im hahetter lebattel haissur.

clarification.explanation: The rule stated — that a forbidden egg remaining whole and closed in its shell does not forbid — is true only for the egg of an impure fowl, or a treifah's or nevelah's egg. But an egg containing a chick embryo forbids even while still entirely closed in its shell, since the chick itself is considered "nevelah" (a dead creature). Likewise, an egg found with a blood spot on the yolk also forbids even while still closed in its shell, since the blood drop constitutes the beginning of the chick's formation, and the blood spreads throughout the entire egg, such that the taste emerging from it is truly the taste of nevelah flesh. Regarding the measure of nullification when cooked in a dish: an egg with blood — sixty against it suffices to nullify it; an egg with an actual chick embryo — some say sixty-one is required (since it is considered like a whole "creature," whose significance adds a unit), and some say sixty suffices even for it; in a case of great monetary loss or urgent need, one may be lenient following the second view. And as stated before, here too the shell of the forbidden egg counts toward the permitted side in the nullification.
takeaways: An egg with a chick embryo or a blood spot forbids even while closed in its shell, unlike an ordinary forbidden egg.
An egg with blood — sixty suffices to nullify; an egg with an embryo — disputed between sixty and sixty-one, and in a pressing situation one may be lenient.

paragraphs: Eprocha shennolad mibbetzat nebela o terepa, hare zeh muttar gamur. veyesh omerim sheen lehoshib lekattechilla tarnegolet al betze terepa, mishshum deen lebattel haissur lekattechilla; veyesh mattirin bazeh lekattechilla. vehammeqel, yesh lo al mi lismok. veayyen "erek-hashshulchan", ot v'.

clarification.explanation: A chick hatched from a nevelah's or treifah's egg is entirely permitted for eating, with no concern at all. But there is disagreement regarding a case where treifah eggs are deliberately placed under a hen from the outset so it broods on them and hatches chicks from them — some say this should not be done as the primary practice, since one should not deliberately and knowingly cause a prohibition to be nullified from the outset; and some permit even this manner. One who wishes to be lenient has authorities to rely upon.
takeaways: A chick already hatched from a nevelah's/treifah's egg is entirely permitted for eating.
Deliberately setting a hen on treifah eggs from the outset to raise chicks is disputed, and the lenient view has authorities to rely upon.

paragraphs: Im hinnichu eper biqdera sheshshalequ bah habbetzim, venimtza sham betza sheyyesh bah eprocha o betza sheyyesh bah dam bachelmon - katab harab "edut bihosep" samon za"l, siman mb, demuttarot habbetzim hakkesherot, mishshum dehaeper noten taam lipgam babbasar, kemo shekkatab mera"n za"l besiman tz"h, seip d. vekatab harab hannizkar deken nohagim bammaarab kesheyyesh chuppa o mila, sheshsholeqin harbeh betzim lechalleq libne-adam, notenin eper betok hammayim sheshsholeqin bahem habbetzim, veaz keshennimtzet ben habbetzim betza sheyyesh bah dam o eprocha, mattirim shear habbetzim, shari mah sheppaleta habbetza haya taam pagum "y haeper hannibla bah, ayyen sham. veken poh irenu bagdad y" yesh gam ken minhag zeh, kesheshsholeqin betzim harbeh beyachad, notenin eper betok hammayim, kede sheim yimmatze aach"k betza sheyyesh bah eprocha o dam, lo yaasru habbetzim hakkesherot. vegam lepi hamminhag tzarik lehannicha haeper betok hammayim sheyyarticha al haesh qodem sheyyannichu habbetzim; vegam tzarik lehannicha eper harbeh sheyyihyeh tamo nikkar bammayim. vehinneh, "g daanan attakka demera"n za"l samekinan bedin desiman tz"h hannizkar, vela chayeshinan lemaen dipligi bazeh, ukemo shekkatab haggaon chida" za"l b"shiyyure-beraka", besiman tz"h, shekkatab depashat hamminhag kedaat mera"n za"l - mikkol maqom minhag zeh shel din habbetzim hannizkar yesh legamgem, ubiprat bedin betza shennimtza bah dam. al ken - "g deen limchot beyad hannohagin bebetzim hetter "y eper - shomer napsho yachush bazeh, vetabo alayv beraka, ki yesh pitchon peh lechalleq ben din habbetzim hannizkar uben din mera"n za"l desiman tz"h.

clarification.explanation: If ash was placed in the pot used to cook eggs, and among them was found an egg with a chick embryo or an egg with blood in the yolk — Rabbi "Edut BeYehosef" wrote that the kosher eggs are permitted, since the ash causes a "spoiling taste" (the taste emerging from the forbidden egg is spoiled and not considered a proper taste, and therefore does not forbid). This is practiced in Morocco, especially at events like a wedding or circumcision, when a large quantity of eggs is cooked for distribution, and ash is added to the water to avoid the need to disqualify all the eggs if a problematic one is found among them. In Baghdad too there was a similar custom — putting a large amount of ash into the boiling water before adding the eggs, so the ash's taste would be noticeable. Although the Ben Ish Chai notes that generally one relies on Maran's ruling regarding "a spoiling taste," he nevertheless expresses some hesitation about this custom — especially regarding an egg found with blood in it — and therefore, although one should not protest against those who follow this practice, "one who guards his soul should be concerned about this, and blessing will come upon him," since there is room to distinguish between the law of eggs and the general law of a spoiling taste.
takeaways: Adding ash to the cooking water turns the taste of a forbidden egg into a "spoiling taste" that does not forbid — a common custom in many communities.
The Ben Ish Chai notes room for stringency here, and one who wishes should be concerned about it even though one should not protest against those who are lenient.

paragraphs: Betza shennoleda beyom tob shennitbashshela im betzim acherot, vehi ushear habbetzim kullan qelippatan shelema - "g dekatabnu leel im haqqelippa shelema, muttar, deeno noten taam, dehanniplat mayya debee bealema ihu, mikkol maqom mashshehu miha ikka, vedabar sheyyesh lo mattirim, bemino oser bemashshehu, al-ken asurot kol habbetzim bo bayyom, ukemo shekkatab harab "erek-hashshulchan" besiman tz"ch, ot v'; vekatab deken hu daat mera"n za"l beorach chayyim, siman tqy"g, yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: An egg laid on a Festival, cooked together with other eggs — when both it and the other eggs remain entirely whole in their shells: although it was stated earlier that an egg in a whole shell imparts no taste and forbids nothing (since what emerges is only "mere water"), there is nevertheless something minute that does emerge. And by the rule that "a thing that has permitters" (here: a Festival-day egg, which has a future "permission" — it will become permitted the next day) forbids even in the most minute amount — all the eggs in the dish are forbidden on that very day (the Festival on which it was laid), but will become permitted the next day.
takeaways: An egg laid on a Festival is forbidden that day (muktzeh), and even if cooked with other whole-shelled eggs, it forbids them due to the minute amount that emerges, since it is "a thing that has permitters."
The other eggs will become permitted the next day, once the Festival-day egg itself becomes permitted.
